transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-09-03
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (NovaCore ML Infra), Elena Rodriguez (NovaCore SRE), Ben Turner (NovaCore Research)
---
Summary (auto): deep dive on GPU runtime profiling, kernel selection, TRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs, KV cache and batching tradeoffs. Action items captured at end.
---
Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to run through a pretty deep technical profiling session on your runtime concerns, specifically kernel selection, TRT-LLM vs vLLM, and CUDA graphs. Priya will drive the tech bits.
[00:18] Priya: Yep hi, thanks. Samir, do you want to give a quick recap of what you saw in your runs? I looked at the logs you sent but wanted to make sure we're aligned on the workload: 8k context, mostly chat-like prompts, batch sizes 1-8, mixed-length sequences?
[00:32] Samir: Yeah that's right. Most traffic is 1-2 prompt turns but we do occasional long in-context examples up to 6k tokens. We saw pretty big variance in p50 vs p95 when we enabled batching — p50 great, but p95 spiked.
[00:46] Ben: Also we tried vLLM baseline and a TensorRT-LLM build from a partner; the TensorRT build had better throughput but latency tail seemed worse at times, and there were spikes around cache misses.
[01:05] Priya: Cool. That matches typical tradeoffs. First thing: kernel selection. Our runtime picks kernels based on layer shape, sequence length distribution, and whether KV cache is warm. There's heuristics for choosing cuBLAS/cudnn exec paths vs custom kernels optimized for attention. When sequence length is short, small matmul kernels win; for long seqs we prefer fused attention with optimized memory layout.
[01:28] Elena: When you say "heuristics" — is that static at model compile time or dynamic at runtime? We need deterministic perf for SLAs.
[01:36] Priya: Good q. It's hybrid. The compiler does a profile pass during an initial warmup to select kernels, but we also have a lightweight runtime selector that can switch kernels on the fly when it detects a significant shift in sequence length or batch distribution. We try to avoid thrashing by hysteresis windows.
[01:53] Samir: That makes sense. In our tests we saw a step-change when going from batch 2 to batch 8, which aligned with a kernel switch — it explained the p95 spike. Is there a way to pin kernel choices?
[02:05] Priya: Yes, you can pin via a model config flag (kernel_overrides) in the runtime; for Private deployments we often recommend pinning for critical routes to avoid runtime re-selection. We'll share the doc.
[02:18] Alex: Let's talk TRT-LLM vs vLLM. Priya, quick summary?
[02:23] Priya: Sure. vLLM is great at scheduling and dynamic batching for throughput, and its KV cache management is focused on on-CPU caching for some setups; TensorRT-LLM shifts more work into fused GPU kernels and leverages TensorRT optimizations and kernels, which often improves raw throughput and per-token GPU efficiency — especially for dense fp16 paths. However, TRT builds can suffer on tail latency if cache misses cause unfused fallback or kernel launch overheads. Also TensorRT's kernel choices are less dynamic unless you implement multi-profile strategies.
[02:53] Ben: We noticed the TRT run had higher throughput for bulk evals but worse p95 for latency-sensitive chat. Is that because of CUDA graph warmup?
[03:02] Priya: Partly. CUDA graphs help amortize kernel launch overhead by capturing a static graph for a sequence of ops. If your request patterns align with captured graphs (sequence length, batch size), you get great latency and throughput. If the workload deviates, you either fall back to non-graph execution or you have to re-capture graphs which is expensive. So variability in input shapes makes CUDA graph benefits brittle unless you design multiple graph variants.
[03:26] Samir: Did you say re-capture is expensive? We saw a ~200ms hit during re-capture in one test which killed p95.
[03:34] Priya: Yeah that's real. Re-capture involves kernel launches to probe configurations and building the graph; we try to schedule captures during low traffic or use background warmers. For interactive workloads, we recommend a small set of canonical graphs covering most common shapes and a fast non-graph fallback for anomalies.
[03:52] Elena: Can the runtime switch between graphs without stopping inflight requests? We need no downtime.
[03:58] Priya: We support hot-swap of pre-captured graphs; the tricky bit is ensuring memory layouts and cached KV slots match. We do a swap that's atomic for new requests, but in-flight ones finish on the old path.
[04:11] Ben: On KV cache, our pattern includes prefix cache (session context) and per-request dynamic KV. We saw eviction and cache thrash when many sessions were active — memory footprint spiked and latency suffered. Any best practices?
[04:23] Priya: A few: limit max cached tokens per session, maintain an LRU with eviction thresholds, and use prefix deduping for repeated system messages. Also quantized caches (storing KV in lower precision) can save GPU DRAM but impacts perf depending on compute path. For Private deployments with large model sizes, we often offload cold KV pages to host memory and keep hot KV on GPU. That adds a hop but is better than OOM.
[04:49] Samir: We noted some inaccurate naming in the logs — like "kv-cache miss" vs "prefix-miss" — are those standard?
[04:56] Priya: Logs can be inconsistent across stacks; we'll share a mapping table. We'll also send a small instrumentation patch for clearer metrics.
[05:05] Alex: Quantization — you ran INT8 experiments, right Samir? What did you see?
[05:10] Samir: We did GPTQ-style offline int8 and also tried per-channel calibration. Throughput improved about 1.6x on average vs fp16 for some kernels, but quality for certain tasks dropped (hallucination increased). Also certain kernels didn't have INT8 fused attention implementations so parts fell back to fp16 which hurts latency.
[05:30] Priya: That's expected: quantization lifts throughput but complexity comes from mixed-kernel paths. For production we recommend a layered approach: first optimize fp16 fused kernels and CUDA graphs, then try selective quantization on less critical sublayers; keep a validation set.
[05:46] Ben: Regarding kernel selection heuristics — do you use cost-modeling (roofline-like) or purely empirical probes?
[05:53] Priya: Hybrid again. We have a cost model tuned to hardware (memory bandwidth vs compute) and we augment it with empirical microbenchmarks during a warm-up phase. The model shortlists candidates and probes confirm actual runtimes. This keeps the probe count manageable.
[06:07] Samir: For our private on-prem target we have A100s and some Ampere/older GPUs. How much do kernel choices differ across arch?
[06:15] Priya: Quite a bit. Newer Ampere/Blackwell archs have different tensor core throughput and better fp8/advanced int8 support. Kernels compiled for one arch may be suboptimal on another. For Private deployments we recommend per-cluster tuning and caching of kernel manifests.
[06:29] Elena: Any gotchas with MIG or multi-tenant GPUs? We were thinking of dedicating slices to teams.
[06:35] Priya: MIG adds isolation but limits the max kernel size and tensor core configuration; some fused kernels expect full GPU memory and might not fit. It can be great for small models or inference with tight tenancy, but you'll need to test workloads per MIG shape.
[06:47] Alex: Let's dig into profiling tools. What did you use for the runs?
[06:52] Ben: We used Nsight Systems for end-to-end tracing, nvprof for kernel times, and a custom microbench harness that runs isolated attention kernels. We also captured CUDA graph capture timings.
[07:05] Priya: Good. We recommend trace levels: layer-level counters, kernel-level traces, and a perf sweep that logs launch times and memory copies. A tip: enable async_memcopy tracing to see host<->device stalls — those often explain hidden latency.
[07:20] Samir: We noticed host pinned memory helped reduce spikes. Is that a general recommendation?
[07:25] Priya: Pinned memory reduces host-device transfer latency variance. For VPC/on-prem with kube devices, make sure drivers and ML stacks are consistent across nodes; inconsistent drivers can cause subtle perf cliffs.
[07:38] Elena: Regarding CUDA graphs and dynamic shapes, is there tooling to auto-generate canonical graph variants?
[07:44] Priya: We have a small auto-capture tool that runs through your representative input shapes and attempts to create the minimal set of graphs to cover X% of traffic. We'll share it; it's part of the tuning checklist.
[07:56] Ben: When capturing multiple graphs, how do you route incoming requests to the right graph efficiently? Pattern matching on sequence length?
[08:03] Priya: Yes, routing based on sequence length + batch size and a hash of request signature. We keep a small decision tree so selection overhead is negligible.
[08:12] Samir: We talked about fallback strategies — say a request doesn't match any graph — you run non-graph path?
[08:17] Priya: Exactly. Non-graph path is slower but robust. Another strategy is to have a fast path that truncates/pads to the nearest canonical shape if your application tolerates it.
[08:28] Alex: Any kernel-level optimizations we should try? Fused QKV, rotary embeddings, custom GEMM shapes?
[08:34] Priya: Fused QKV and fused attention with packed bias definitely helps. Rotary embedding handling can be optimized by precomputing rotation factors in a fused kernel. Also check for GEMM tiling shapes — sometimes tiling that matches tensor cores yields 1.1-1.4x gains. We can share kernel-level knobs.
[08:53] Ben: We tried changing tiling but driver rewrites made results inconsistent. How stable are these gains?
[08:59] Priya: Gains vary by driver & CUDA version. Always lock driver/CUDA/cuDNN versions for production and test across upgrades. We'll provide a compatibility matrix.
[09:09] Samir: For our model (~70B) memory is the real constraint. Do you recommend sharding KV across GPUs or offloading?
[09:16] Priya: For that scale, common patterns: tensor parallel model sharding with local KV per device; or keep a single replica but offload cold KV to host; or use NVLink-backed KV sharing. Sharding preserves latency but requires network fabric tuning. Offload reduces GPU DRAM but adds host hops. We'll discuss tradeoffs in the follow-up doc.
[09:37] Elena: Security question: for private VPC deployments, will kernel-level profiling leak model info? We need audit controls.
[09:44] Priya: Profiling artifacts shouldn't contain model weights, but traces can reveal sequence lengths and perf patterns. We recommend anonymizing traces and storing them with encryption (KMS/HSM) and RBAC. Redwood Private supports encrypted traces and role-limited access.
[09:58] Alex: On the topic of operator ergonomics: how do we expose these knobs without overwhelming product teams?
[10:03] Priya: Two layers: auto-tune for most routes, and an advanced config UI for pinned kernels/graphs for critical routes. Also have profiling-as-a-service: when you report a perf regression, we automatically run a targeted probe.
[10:15] Samir: About the regression, we saw a perf regression after a model patch; what's the usual cause?
[10:21] Priya: Changed attention implementation, different operator fusion pattern, or increased context-length for some tests. We couple rolling evals to detect regressions — Redwood has a regression alert tied to a prompt set.
[10:33] Ben: Some other specifics: were there issues with memory fragmentation causing OOM deltas?
[10:38] Priya: Yes, fragmentation is real. We recommend periodic allocator resets during low traffic or using a custom allocator that avoids fragmentation for transient KV pages.
[10:47] Elena: One more on batching: we want to preserve low latency for interactive queries but still benefit from batching. How to tune?
[10:55] Priya: Use a latency SLO-driven autoscaling and dynamic batching with a cap on aggregation delay (e.g., max 10ms). For higher throughput routes, increase batch windows. Also micro-batching combined with async invocation can help.
[11:07] Samir: We saw that increasing batch size changed kernel selection to a slower variant for p95. Is there a guidance for safe batch thresholds?
[11:14] Priya: Benchmark at multiple batch sizes and choose a knee point where throughput gains saturate and latency tails remain acceptable. Often batch sizes 2-4 for chat workloads; larger for bulk inference. We'll include charts.
[11:26] Alex: Quick interjection: we'll make sure the benchmark harness includes p50/p90/p95 and also memory & kernel profiles per layer.
[11:33] Ben: In earlier files we saw 'cudagraph capture failed' logs. Any common root causes?
[11:39] Priya: Mismatched stream ordering, dynamic shape divergence, or unsupported ops in the proposed graph. Use a minimal graph capture and ensure deterministic streams. We can share a debug checklist.
[11:51] Samir: On operator fallbacks — when a kernel is missing for fp8 or int8, does the runtime insert a fallback to fp16 and keep executing?
[11:58] Priya: Yes, we have mixed-precision fallback paths. Runtime emits telemetry when fallbacks occur. For critical routes we recommend pinning to a known-good precision set.
[12:08] Elena: Can Redwood's profiler annotate traces to show the kernel choice reason (cost-model vs probe)?
[12:13] Priya: Yes, we surface the selection reason in the trace metadata — either 'cost-model', 'probe-confirmed', or 'override'.
[12:20] Ben: Great. Let's talk about the exact benchmark experiments we should run in the joint test: list of runs?
[12:26] Priya: Suggestion: (1) Baseline vLLM fp16 no-graphs single-instance, batch sweep 1-16; (2) TensorRT-LLM fp16 with graphs, canonical shapes only; (3) TensorRT-LLM with multi-graph capture covering 95% shapes; (4) Selective int8/GPTQ runs for off-critical paths; (5) KV offload vs local KV tests; (6) MIG shape tests if you run MIG. We'll produce a harness script.
[12:54] Samir: Good. For metrics we want p50/p90/p95, tokens/sec, GPU util, memory high-water, and capture times.
[13:03] Priya: We'll add kernel-level stats: kernel time breakdown, launch overhead, and memory copy times. Also include a diff of kernel manifests between runs.
[13:13] Alex: Any gotchas if NovaCore wants to run on-prem across multiple node types?
[13:18] Priya: Heterogeneous clusters complicate kernel caching. We recommend per-node-class manifests and a scheduler that pins jobs to compatible nodes. We'll share scheduler hints.
[13:28] Ben: A note on TensorRT licensing/partners — we had to fumble some licensing to get the partner TRT-LLM build. Any legal caveats?
[13:35] Alex: We won't dive deep here, but we'll surface any licensing notes in the security package — many enterprise customers already use TRT internally but check export/compliance.
[13:44] Samir: A few logs we saw referenced 'launcher: cudnn exec 0x3f' which wasn't in any doc — is that internal?
[13:50] Priya: Some low-level exec IDs are internal to certain kernel libraries. We'll add mappings.
[13:56] Elena: About observability — can we get per-route kernel manifests in the console?
[14:01] Priya: Yes, Redwood Console can display per-route kernel manifests and also diff them across deploys.
[14:08] Ben: We also want alerts when a kernel fallback happens frequently. Possible?
[14:12] Priya: Already possible — alert on telemetry thresholds (e.g., >5% requests causing fallback).
[14:19] Samir: One practical question: what's the recommended way to test CUDA graph coverage quickly?
[14:24] Priya: Run the auto-capture with a representative traffic sample for ~30 minutes; it reports coverage and suggested canonical shapes. We'll provide the script.
[14:35] Alex: Switching to more hands-on -- Priya, can you walk through a short demo of a kernel trace you shared earlier?
[14:40] Priya: Sure, I'll share my screen (note: placeholder for actual screen share link).
[14:48] [screen share noises / short pause]
[15:00] Priya: Here's an example trace: layer 12 attention kernel dominated runtime; you can see GPU shows many small kernel launches; after fusing QKV we reduced number of launches and gained 30% in that layer. The trace also shows capture time when we re-captured graphs.
[15:20] Ben: Could you zoom on the small launches — are those duplicate kernels due to split heads implementation?
[15:25] Priya: Yes, the split-head approach caused multiple small GEMMs. Fused implementation reduced launches by merging them.
[15:31] Samir: We saw in one trace a high time on cudaMemcpyAsync — host->device — is that due to KV offload?
[15:37] Priya: Likely. That indicates hot->cold KV migrations or too-frequent host staging. Consider batching those transfers or using pinned memory as discussed.
[15:47] Alex: We are at about 35 minutes — any other customer-specific constraints we should capture?
[15:52] Samir: Our security team requires all traces at rest encrypted with our KMS and RBAC limited. Also training infra can't be co-located with inference due to compliance, so dedicated clusters are preferred.
[16:03] Priya: Noted. For Private we support KMS integration and dedicated clusters. We'll document the deployment topology we recommend.
[16:12] Ben: Let's finish with a concrete experiment plan and timeline.
[16:16] Alex: Proposed timeline: this week — share checklist and harness; next week — NovaCore uploads model and runs baseline; week after — Redwood runs TRT-LLM builds and we compare. Does that work?
[16:28] Samir: Sounds good. One more quick question on auto-batching: do we support deadline-based batching (i.e., max-wait ms)?
[16:34] Priya: Yes, deadline-based batching with a max-wait parameter. Set conservative values for chat to minimize tail.
[16:40] Ben: Anything else on the kernel selection policy?
[16:43] Priya: We'll include a diagram showing the selection flow: cost-model shortlist -> probe -> confirm -> pin or runtime switch with hysteresis.
[16:52] Alex: Okay let's capture the next steps. (recap) Priya will share the TensorRT tuning checklist and auto-capture tool, Alex will stand up the test harness cluster, NovaCore will upload model and sample prompts, and we'll schedule a follow-up.
[17:06] Samir: Thanks everyone.
[17:09] Elena: Thanks, bye.
[17:10] Ben: Bye.
